title: You Keep Asking God to Change Them—What If the Prayer He Wants to Answer First Is You?
paragraphs: You Keep Asking God to Change Them—What If the Prayer He Wants to Answer First Is You?
You have prayed about their attitude, their failures, their words, their coldness, their stubbornness. But what happens when Jesus quietly turns the prayer around—and asks you to look in the mirror?
There is a prayer that can sound deeply spiritual while keeping us safely hidden.
“God, change them.”
Change my husband.
Change my wife.
Change my parents.
Change my child.
Change my friend.
Change that person who betrayed me.
Change the person who refuses to apologize.
Change the person who keeps hurting me.
Change the person who cannot seem to see what everyone else can see.
And sometimes that prayer is completely appropriate.
People really do sin against us.

People really can be selfish, cruel, manipulative, dishonest, neglectful, proud, or destructive. Scripture never commands us to pretend evil is good simply because admitting we have our own sins feels more “humble.” Biblical self-examination is not denial of another person’s wrongdoing.
But there is an uncomfortable moment that can happen in prayer.
You begin talking to God about everything wrong with them...
and somehow God begins dealing with you.
You came carrying evidence.
He brings a mirror.
You came ready to explain what they did.
He begins touching your pride.
You came asking Him to expose their selfishness.
He begins exposing your bitterness.
You wanted Him to confront their words.
He reminds you of yours.
You wanted justice for the way they wounded you.
He begins asking what you have been feeding in your heart since the wound happened.
And suddenly the prayer you thought was about them becomes frighteningly personal.
Jesus spoke directly into this instinct:

“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye.”
Matthew 7:3–5
The Greek makes the image almost impossible to soften.
Jesus speaks of the κάρφος — karphos, the speck or small bit of material in your brother’s eye.
Then He speaks of the δοκός — dokos in your own.
A beam.
A large piece of timber.
The contrast is deliberately startling.
There you are, leaning toward someone else’s face, carefully diagnosing the tiny object obstructing their vision...
while somehow ignoring the timber obstructing yours.
It is almost comedic.
Until you realize Jesus is describing us.
We can become extraordinarily observant when someone else is wrong.
We remember dates.
Words.
Screenshots.
Tone of voice.
Promises they broke.
Things they should have noticed.
Things they should have said.
Things they should never have said.
We can reconstruct the entire argument while washing dishes.
We can retry the case while driving.
We can deliver imaginary closing arguments in the shower.
And somehow, in every reenactment, we remain remarkably reasonable.
They remain remarkably guilty.
That is the unwanted mirror of Matthew 7.
Jesus is not merely asking, “Did they sin?”
He is asking:
Can you still see yourself clearly?
That question can hurt more than the argument.
Because there are seasons when another person truly has behaved badly, yet their wrongdoing has slowly become permission for ours.
“They made me angry.”
“They pushed me this far.”
“If they respected me, I wouldn’t talk like this.”
“If they apologized, I wouldn’t be bitter.”
“If they changed, I could finally become peaceful again.”
Listen carefully to what has happened.
Your spiritual condition has been placed into somebody else’s hands.
Your obedience is waiting for their obedience.
Your repentance is waiting for their repentance.
Your peace is waiting for their behavior.
Your tenderness is waiting for their apology.
Your holiness is waiting for them to become easier to love.
And Jesus loves you too much to leave you there.
He does not say the speck does not exist.
This matters.
Matthew 7:5 does not end with Jesus saying, “Forget your brother’s eye.”
He says first remove the log from your own eye, “and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye.”
The goal is not moral blindness.
It is clear sight.
The Greek verb translated “you will see clearly” is διαβλέψεις — diablepseis.
The issue is vision.
Jesus is confronting the kind of hypocrisy that can recognize another person’s problem without recognizing how badly our own sin has distorted our sight.
That means Matthew 7 is not teaching, “Nobody may ever correct anybody.”

Jesus Himself confronted sin. The apostles confronted sin. The New Testament teaches believers to restore those caught in transgression—but to do so with gentleness while watching ourselves lest we also be tempted (Galatians 6:1).
Christian correction begins differently from self-righteous accusation.
It begins before God.
It begins with the terrifying possibility:
“Lord, show me where I am wrong too.”
That is a dangerous prayer for your ego.
But it may save your soul from becoming hardened.
Because pride wants a courtroom.
Grace brings you to a cross.
Pride wants evidence against somebody else.
Grace asks what needs crucifying in you.
Pride says, “Look what they did.”
Repentance says, “Jesus, search me too.”
And maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you are reading this while thinking about one specific person.
You know exactly who they are.
Perhaps you have prayed for months that God would change them.
Maybe years.
And perhaps they genuinely need to change.
So keep praying for them.
But tonight, add another prayer.
“Jesus... what about me?”
Not because everything is your fault.
Not because their sin suddenly becomes acceptable.
Not because forgiveness requires you to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Not because biblical humility means surrendering boundaries or pretending betrayal never happened.
But because someone else’s sin cannot become your permission to resist Christ.
Ask Him:
Where has hurt become bitterness?
Where has disappointment become contempt?
Where has discernment become superiority?
Where has correction become punishment?
Where has silence become manipulation?
Where has “protecting myself” become refusing to forgive?
Where have I exaggerated their faults and minimized mine?
Where am I demanding from them a repentance I am unwilling to practice myself?
That prayer changes things.
Sometimes it changes the relationship.
Sometimes it does not.
Sometimes the other person still refuses responsibility.
Sometimes reconciliation is possible.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
Sometimes forgiveness happens without restored trust because repentance and trustworthy fruit have not followed.
Christian grace does not require pretending consequences are unnecessary.
But something profound happens when you stop making another person's transformation a prerequisite for your own obedience.
You become free to obey Jesus now.
You can repent now.
You can forgive before you receive the apology you imagined.
You can refuse revenge now.
You can stop rehearsing hatred now.
You can confess your words now.
You can make restitution where necessary now.
You can become more like Christ even while another person is still resisting Him.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
You may have been right about what they did and still be wrong about what you became because of it.
Read that again.
Because being wounded does not automatically make every response righteous.
The cross destroys our favorite categories.
At Calvary, nobody gets to stand before Jesus boasting, “At least I wasn't as bad as them.”
Scripture says:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23
All.
Your enemy.
Your spouse.
Your parents.
Your children.
Your pastor.
Your friend.
The person who wounded you.
And you.
And me.
But the Gospel does not stop with exposure.
Thank God it does not stop there.
Because if Christianity were only a mirror showing us how sinful we are, eventually every honest person would despair.
The mirror prepares us to see our need for the Savior.
Jesus does not expose the beam in your eye because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes what is destroying your sight because He came to save sinners.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God took upon Himself the judgment sinners deserved.
Jesus did not die because we successfully proved somebody else was worse.
He died because we needed mercy.
He rose again because death would not have the final word.
And now the invitation is not:
“Fix yourself so Jesus will accept you.”
It is:
“Come to Jesus. Repent. Believe. Receive mercy. Then let His grace begin transforming the places you have spent years defending.”
The Greek word so often translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one’s mind, turning from the old way, reorienting oneself toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty.
Judas felt anguish.
Pharaoh regretted consequences.
Repentance turns.
Repentance stops negotiating with the sin.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, You are right about me.”
And grace answers:
“Come.”
Maybe that is the word you needed.
Not condemnation.
Come.
Come out from behind the evidence.
Come out from behind the screenshots.
Come out from behind what they did five years ago.
Come out from behind the sentence, “But they started it.”
Bring the anger.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the betrayal.
Bring the marriage that does not look like you imagined.
Bring the friendship that broke.
Bring the family wound nobody understands.
Bring the apology you never received.
Bring the things you wish you had never said.
Bring the version of yourself you hardly recognize anymore.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
There is enough mercy at the cross for what they did.
And there is enough mercy for what you did too.
That is the scandal of grace.
Nobody arrives righteous.
Nobody purchases forgiveness.
Nobody earns resurrection.
We come empty-handed.
And Christ rewrites everything.
Perhaps the miracle you have been asking God for really does begin with the other person changing.
God can do that.
Pray for it.
But perhaps the first miracle He wants to perform is quieter.
The miracle of making you tender again.
The miracle of teaching you to apologize without adding “but you...”
The miracle of letting you hear correction without immediately building a defense.
The miracle of giving you enough security in Christ that admitting you were wrong no longer feels like death.
The miracle of forgiving somebody who may never understand what their actions cost you.
The miracle of boundaries without hatred.
Truth without cruelty.
Correction without superiority.
Discernment without contempt.
Conviction without despair.
Grace without pretending sin does not matter.
Maybe the prayer changes tonight.
“Lord, change them.”
Pause.
“And Jesus...
change me too.”
Search what I defend.
Expose what I excuse.
Show me the beam I cannot see because I have spent too long staring at their speck.
Make me quick to repent.
Slow to accuse.
Faithful to truth.
Generous with mercy.
And unwilling to call bitterness “discernment” simply because somebody really did hurt me.
Make me look like You.
That prayer may not instantly repair your relationship.
But it can begin transforming you.
And transformation is exactly what grace does.
If this article put a name to something you have been hiding, don't rush past the discomfort.
Stay there with Jesus.
Open Matthew 7 again.
Read verses 1–5 slowly.
Then pray without mentioning the other person for a few minutes.
That may be harder than you expect.
Ask only:
“Jesus, what are You showing me about me?”
And listen.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a sentence earns grace.
But as an honest confession that you no longer want everybody else's sin to distract you from the transforming work Christ wants to do in your own heart.
There are moments when believers do not need another argument.
They need brothers and sisters willing to carry them before God.
Please do not send Matthew 7 to somebody as another way of saying, “See? Jesus agrees that you're the problem.”
That would be an almost painfully ironic way to use this passage.
They may desperately need to discover that repentance is not humiliation.
In Christ, repentance is a doorway home.
It cannot.
Scripture makes no such claim.

But if you want another practical way to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, you can help Gospel-centered truth reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church but will stop for a story on their screen.
Your support helps us keep writing, sharing Scripture, encouraging struggling believers, reaching seekers, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
Send it privately to the person who keeps blaming everyone because looking inward feels unbearable.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person quietly losing faith.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the Christian who knows all the right language but has forgotten how to repent.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is about religious people pretending they are better than everybody else.
Let them discover the opposite.
Christianity begins with sinners admitting we cannot save ourselves.
Then Jesus steps into the scandal.
With truth.
With wounds in His hands.
With mercy we could never purchase.
With grace we could never deserve.
And He begins rewriting people.
Maybe even the person you have spent months asking Him to change.
But tonight...
before you say their name again...
stand before the mirror.
Look at the cross.
And whisper:
“Jesus, start with me.”
Because sometimes the answer to “Lord, why won't You change them?” begins when grace whispers back:
“Will you let Me change you?”
